findings.text: Guilt as an objective, transactable status begins with an act, intentional or unintentional: Lev 4:13, 4:22, 4:27, 5:2-5 and 5:17 repeatedly frame this as sins from doing any of the things that ought not to be done, explicitly covering inadvertent breach and not only deliberate wrongdoing.
findings.flag: inferential LLM synthesis; Lev 4:22, 4:27, 5:2-5 and 5:17 are given by number only on this line

findings.text: The guilt is realized: H0816's Leviticus 4-6 verses use and he realizes his guilt as what reads like a near-technical hinge phrase, repeated near-verbatim across Lev 4:13, 4:22, 4:27, 5:2, 5:3, 5:4, 5:5, 5:17, 6:4 and 6:5. Guilt is not complete as a status until it is recognized, not merely incurred.

Guilt accrues as a load: H0819's guilt is already great and incurred guilt more and more (2 Chr 28:13, 33:23), and H5375J's bear your iniquity, guilt or punishment idiom, treat guilt as cumulative weight, not a binary switch.

The load is carried by the guilty party themselves: H5375J's verses split cleanly into two carriers of the same idiom, and in the first the guilty party bears it (Lev 5:17, 17:16, Num 5:31, Num 14:34, the wilderness generation).

The load is transferred onto a substitute, the second carrier of the same H5375J idiom: the scapegoat shall bear all their iniquities (Lev 16:22) and, the same verb, the Servant bore the sin of many (Isa 53:12).

Ezekiel 18:19-20 sits directly against the transfer reading in the other direction: it explicitly denies that a son bears (nasa) his father's iniquity. The same verb is used to assert strict non-transferability of personal guilt in one direction, while other texts in the same set use it for sacrificial transferability in the other; the input data does not resolve this tension and simply contains both uses side by side.

A remedy exists at the institutional level: H0817 is the pivot strong that is both the abstract guilt-word and the name of the sacrifice that removes it (Lev 5:7, 7:5, 14:21, 19:21, 1 Sam 6:17 and, notably, Isa 53:10, where the Servant's soul itself makes an offering for guilt). The guilt-offering is not incidental vocabulary; it is the same lexical item as the guilt it answers.

A separate, forensic register runs in parallel (G1777): the Greek liability sense does not describe a process of realization or a burden carried but names a fixed legal exposure to a specific penalty (liable to judgment, liable to the council, guilty of an eternal sin, guilty of all of it for failing at one point of the law, Jas 2:10). This reads as a different grammatical shape of the same concept: guilt as standing exposed to a verdict, rather than guilt as something building up inside a person.

One verse frames guilt relationally rather than ritually or forensically: H0818's single citation (Gen 42:21) has Joseph's brothers indict themselves for a failure of compassion (we saw the distress of his soul and did not listen), with no offering, no court and no accrual language: guilt as retrospective conscience alone.
